messages.author: d096edb922462595
messages.subject: Question on mirt.model
parts:
Hi Phil,

I am trying to specify a confirmatory model (14 items) in which items 1-7 load onto the first factor only, items 8-14 load onto the second factor only, and discrimination parameters 1 and 8, 2, and 9, and so forth are each constrained to be equal.

I am trying
 
model_constrained_within_country <- mirt.model('F1=1-7
                                 F2=8-14
                                 CONSTRAIN = (1,a1,8,a2), (2,a1,9,a2),(3,a1,10,a2),(4,a1,11,a2),(5,a1,12,a2),(6,a1,13,a2),(7,a1,14,a2)
                                 COV=F1*F2')
but applying this model gives me an error that "constraint is applied to x but should only be applied to estimated parameters. Please fix!". 

What is the correct syntax here?
Many thanks,
Tobi

model_constrained_within_country <- mirt.model('F1=1-7

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: Question on mirt.model
parts: Hey Tobias,

On Wed, Feb 4, 2015 at 3:22 PM, Tobias Konitzer <tobias....@gmail.com> wrote:
Hey Phil,

That is awesome, thanks! The other thing that the package could benefit from would be a canned function for percentage correctly predicted (which can of course be calculated manually, but is a bit tedious),
It's also somewhat trivial. IRT methods predict the intercept extremely well, and therefore the proportion correct will only ever be off by a few decimal points. Not really something worth including.
and a visualization of model fit, maybe similar to http://mdwardlab.com/sites/default/files/GreenhillWardSacks.pdf).

I'm not really sure what to do with this. In M2(), you could return the residual covariance between items, which probably could be passed to something like a bubble-scatterplot or a correlogram to visualize the pattern of residuals, which seems to get at model misfit well enough....but in IRT, items may fit poorly in other ways too, not just in the expected two-way covariances (this is one reason I prefer IRT over approaches like SEM for analysing test items, because SEM only focuses on 2-way covariation rather than looking at each item in isolation for potential problems). Cheers.

Phil

What do you think?

messages.subject: Re: Question on mirt.model
parts:
OK, Agreed with regard to PCP. My point is just that this is an often-reported first take at model fit in many dimensions, and a canned function might help some users here.
 I am not sure why you are hesitant with regard to the separation plot. It is certainly neat for simple logit models, and in a way, if you pool across items IRT is not that different, so it might provide some intuition with regard to misspecification. At any rate, some visualization of overall fit would be a cool thing; I will keep my eyes open as well!

Tobi

messages.subject: Re: Question on mirt.model
parts:
Dear Phil,

See below! Tobi

library(mirt)
library(separationplot)
data(SAT12)
#dichotomize
key <- c(1,4,5,2,3,1,2,1,3,1,2,4,2,1,5,3,4,4,1,4,3,3,4,1,3,5,1,3,1,5,4,5)
dicho.SAT12 <- key2binary(SAT12,key)
mirt_out<- mirt(dicho.SAT12,1)

#predicted values
holder<-matrix(NA, nrow=nrow(dicho.SAT12),ncol=ncol(dicho.SAT12))
colnames(holder)<-colnames(dicho.SAT12)
for (i in 1:ncol(dicho.SAT12)){
  holder[,i]<-plogis(coef(mirt_out)[[i]][2]+coef(mirt_out)[[i]][1]*fscores(mirt_out,full.scores=T, scores.only=T))
}

#PCP pooled over all items
mean(round(as.vector(holder))==as.vector(dicho.SAT12),na.rm=T)

#Separationplot over all items
separationplot(as.vector(holder),as.vector(dicho.SAT12),type='rect')

#separationplot orders all observed answers (1=dark red, 0=light red) according to the model the value predicts (also indicated by the black trace line)
#A perfect model produces a separationplot in which dark red and light red are perfectly separated

messages.subject: Re: Question on mirt.model
parts:
Thanks Tobi, and sorry for the delayed reply (been busy in Europe). I see what you mean here, but I think this is somewhat specific for IRT models in that it really only is applicable to dichotomous tests. It's also not quite invariant in IRT models either because the expected theta values are computed by secondary means (unlike the glm example in the separationplot help files, where the expected values are fixed in the estimation algorithm). So you could get really different results depending on the estimator if the test size is small.

I think it's a neat example though, so I'll add a bit more to it in case others find it useful in the future. The predicted values are really just tracelines, so you could use the prodtrace() function built into mirt like so:

```

library(mirt)
library(separationplot)

data(SAT12)
#dichotomize
key <- c(1,4,5,2,3,1,2,1,3,1,2,4,2,1,5,3,4,4,1,4,3,3,4,1,3,5,1,3,1,5,4,5)
dicho.SAT12 <- key2binary(SAT12,key)
mirt_out <- mirt(dicho.SAT12,1)

#predicted values

fs <- fscores(mirt_out, full.scores=TRUE, scores.only=TRUE, method = 'ML')
holder <- matrix(NA, nrow=nrow(dicho.SAT12),ncol=ncol(dicho.SAT12))

colnames(holder)<-colnames(dicho.SAT12)
for (i in 1:ncol(dicho.SAT12)){

ii <- extract.item(mirt_out, i)
    holder[,i] <- probtrace(ii, fs)[,2L]

}

#PCP pooled over all items

mean(round(as.vector(holder)) == as.vector(dicho.SAT12), na.rm = TRUE)

#Separationplot over all items
separationplot(as.vector(holder), as.vector(dicho.SAT12), type='rect')
```

This will generalize a little nicer if 3PL items were used instead of 2PL. Cheers.

Phil

Hi Phil,

I am trying to specify a confirmatory model (14 items) in which items 1-7 load onto the first factor only, items 8-14 load onto the second factor only, and discrimination parameters 1 and 8, 2, and 9, and so forth are each constrained to be equal.

I am trying
 
model_constrained_within_country <- mirt.model('F1=1-7
                                 F2=8-14
                                 CONSTRAIN = (1,a1,8,a2), (2,a1,9,a2),(3,a1,10,a2),(4,a1,11,a2),(5,a1,12,a2),(6,a1,13,a2),(7,a1,14,a2)
                                 COV=F1*F2')
but applying this model gives me an error that "constraint is applied to x but should only be applied to estimated parameters. Please fix!". 

What is the correct syntax here?

The syntax doesn't support this type of definition yet. You can do something similar with the constrain input, but it's a bit more cumbersome and requires looking at the starting value locations. See something like this example to get an idea of how to do it. http://philchalmers.github.io/mirt/html/Longitudinal-IRT.html

Phil 
 
Many thanks,
Tobi

For something a little more useful to those who want to see how this works for their own data, here's a better function wrapper based on the code I just supplied. Cheers.

````
mirt_sepplot <- function(x, type='rect', ...){
    require(separationplot)
    dat <- x@Data$data
    
    #predicted values
    fs <- fscores(x, full.scores=TRUE, scores.only=TRUE, ...)
    holder <- matrix(NA, nrow=nrow(dat), ncol=ncol(dat))
    colnames(holder) <- colnames(dat)
    for (i in 1:ncol(dat)){

ii <- extract.item(mirt_out, i)
        holder[,i] <- probtrace(ii, fs)[,2L]
    }

#Separationplot over all items
    separationplot(as.vector(holder), as.vector(dat), type=type)
} 


#-------------------------------------------------------------------
#### example
library(mirt)

data(SAT12)
#dichotomize
key <- c(1,4,5,2,3,1,2,1,3,1,2,4,2,1,5,3,4,4,1,4,3,3,4,1,3,5,1,3,1,5,4,5)
dicho.SAT12 <- key2binary(SAT12,key)
mirt_out <- mirt(dicho.SAT12,1)

mirt_sepplot(mirt_out)
mirt_sepplot(mirt_out, method = 'ML')
````
